You are shown a snapshot of US macroeconomic and market data as it was known at the end of one month between 2007 and 2026.

Estimate which month the snapshot describes. Use only the figures supplied plus your general knowledge of economic history.

Reply with one JSON object and nothing else:
{"year": yyyy, "month": m, "confidence": c, "cues": ["...", "..."]}
Rules: year is an integer from 2007 to 2026; month is an integer from 1 to 12; c in [0, 1] is your confidence that the guess is within 6 months of the truth; 1 to 3 short cues citing the inputs.
text:
This looks like the 2008-09 financial crisis, most likely at the equity bottom around March 2009. Several figures fit that period:

- US large-cap equity is down 36.2% over 12 months, with a 1-month rebound of +10.8%. The S&P 500 bottomed on March 9, 2009 and rose about 9% in March, so the 1-month bounce points to March.
- Unemployment is 6.7%, which matches November 2008 (6.8%) or December 2008 (7.3%). That is a bit low for March 2009, when it was 8.5%. Payrolls averaging -419k over 3 months fit November 2008, where the 3-month average was about -400k or worse.
- Headline CPI is +1.01% YoY. October 2008 was 3.7% and November 2008 was 1.1%, so the CPI points to November 2008.
- The fed funds rate is 0.09%, which fits a month after the December 2008 cut. The 10-year yield is 2.11%, consistent with late November or December 2008 (about 2.1-2.2%).
- The VIX is 41.63, and the 1-month equity return is +10.8%. In November 2008 the S&P fell about 7%, but in December 2008 it rose about 1%. Neither matches the +10.8%.
- The 1-month returns of EM +22% and developed ex-US +18.6% are very large. March 2009 had EM up about 9%, so this is more consistent with a different month. October 2008 was very negative, and November 2008 was also negative.
- The rebound could instead come from April 2020. COVID gives a different picture, though: unemployment was 14.7% and the 10-year yield was 0.6%. So COVID does not fit.

Putting this together, the 12-month equity drawdown of -36% and the IG credit +12.1% in 1 month fit a rebound month. The Baa spread of 5.86 pp is very wide, and Baa minus 10-year Treasury hit about 6 pp in December 2008. The dollar is +9.6% YoY. The 10-year yield of 2.11% fits December 2008, and the policy rate of 0.09% also fits December. The unemployment rate of 6.7% does not match December exactly, but it could reflect a different measure or vintage.

For the equity return, December 2008 total return was about +1%. The +10.8% could be a different window, such as the last day of November to a late-December date, or a data quirk. I'll go with December 2008.
